{{for|quasisymmetric functions in algebraic combinatorics|quasisymmetric function}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''quasisymmetric''' [[homeomorphism]] between metric spaces is a map that generalizes [[lipschitz function|bi-Lipschitz]] maps. While bi-Lipschitz maps shrink or expand the diameter of a set by no more than a multiplicative factor, quasisymmetric maps satisfy the weaker geometric property that they preserve the relative sizes of sets: if two sets ''A'' and ''B'' have diameters ''t'' and are no more than distance ''t'' apart, then the ratio of their sizes changes by no more than a multiplicative constant. These maps are also related to [[quasiconformal]] maps, since in many circumstances they are in fact equivalent.<ref>{{cite book| last = Heinonen| first = Juha | title = Lectures on Analysis on Metric Spaces | series = Universitext | publisher = Springer-Verlag | location = New York | year = 2001 | pages = x+140 | isbn = 978-0-387-95104-1}}</ref>

==Definition==

Let <math>(X,d_X)</math> and <math> (Y,d_Y) </math>  be two [[metric space]]s. A [[homeomorphism]] <math> f\colon X\to Y </math>  is said to be '''η-quasisymmetric''' for some increasing function <math> \eta:[0,+\infty) \to [0,+\infty) </math> if for any triple <math> x,y,z </math>  of distinct points in <math> X </math>, we have:

<math> \frac{d_Y(f(x),f(y))}{d_{Y}(f(x),f(z))} \leq \eta\left(\frac{d_X(x,y)}{d_X(x,z)}\right). </math>


==Basic properties==

; Inverses are quasisymmetric : If <math> f\colon X\to Y </math> is an invertible ''η''-quasisymmetric map as above, then its inverse map is <math>\eta'</math>-quasisymmetric, where <math display=inline>\eta'(t) = 1/\eta^{-1}(1/t).</math>
; Quasisymmetric maps preserve relative sizes of sets : If <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are subsets of <math>X</math> and <math>A</math> is a subset of <math>B</math>, then
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{2}\eta^{-1}\left(\frac{\operatorname{diam} B}{\operatorname{diam} A}\right)\leq \frac{\operatorname{diam}f(B)}{\operatorname{diam}f(A)}\leq 2\eta\left(\frac{\operatorname{diam} B}{\operatorname{diam}A}\right).</math>

==Examples==

===Weakly quasisymmetric maps===

A map <math> f\colon X\to Y </math> is said to be '''H-weakly-quasisymmetric''' for some <math>H>0</math> if for all triples of distinct points <math>x,y,z</math> in <math>X</math>, then
<math display="block"> |f(x)-f(y)|\leq H|f(x)-f(z)|\;\;\;\text{ whenever }\;\;\; |x-y|\leq |x-z|</math>

Not all weakly quasisymmetric maps are quasisymmetric. However, if <math>X</math> is [[Connected space|connected]] and <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are [[doubling measures and metric spaces|doubling]], then all weakly quasisymmetric maps are quasisymmetric. The appeal of this result is that proving weak-quasisymmetry is much easier than proving quasisymmetry directly, and in many natural settings the two notions are equivalent.

===δ-monotone maps===

A [[Monotone map#Monotonicity in functional analysis|monotone map]] <math> f\colon H\to H </math> on a [[Hilbert space]] <math> H </math> is '''δ-monotone''' if for all <math> x,y </math> in <math> H </math>,
<math display="block"> \langle f(x)-f(y),x-y\rangle\geq \delta |f(x)-f(y)|\cdot|x-y|.</math>

To grasp what this condition means geometrically, suppose <math> f(0)=0 </math> and consider the above estimate when <math> y=0 </math>. Then it implies that the angle between the vector <math> x </math>  and its image <math> f(x) </math>  stays between 0 and <math> \arccos(\delta)<\pi/2 </math>.

These maps are quasisymmetric, although they are a much narrower subclass of quasisymmetric maps. For example, while a general quasisymmetric map in the complex plane could map the real line to a set of [[Hausdorff dimension]] strictly greater than one, a ''δ''-monotone will always map the real line to a rotated [[Graph of a function|graph]] of a Lipschitz function <math>L:\mathbb{R} \rarr \mathbb{R}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Kovalev | first = Leonid V. | title= Quasiconformal geometry of monotone mappings | journal = Journal of the London Mathematical Society | volume = 75 | year = 2007 | number = 2 | pages = 391–408 | doi=10.1112/jlms/jdm008| citeseerx = 10.1.1.194.2458 }}</ref>

==Doubling measures==

===The real line===

Quasisymmetric homeomorphisms of the [[real line]] to itself can be characterized in terms of their derivatives.<ref>{{cite journal| last = Beurling | first = A. |author-link=Arne Beurling |author2=Ahlfors, L. |authorlink2=Lars Ahlfors  | title = The boundary correspondence under quasiconformal mappings | journal = Acta Math. | volume=  96 | year = 1956 | pages = 125–142| doi=10.1007/bf02392360| doi-access = free }}</ref> An increasing homeomorphism <math>f:\mathbb{R} \rarr \mathbb{R}</math> is quasisymmetric if and only if there is a constant <math>C>0  </math>  and  a [[doubling measures and metric spaces|doubling measure]] ''μ'' on the real line such that

<math display="block"> f(x)=C+\int_0^x \, d\mu(t).</math>

===Euclidean space===

An analogous result holds in Euclidean space. Suppose <math> C=0 </math>  and we rewrite the above equation for <math> f </math>  as 
<math display="block"> f(x) = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\frac{x-t}{|x-t|}+\frac{t}{|t|}\right)d\mu(t).</math>

Writing it this way, we can attempt to define a map using this same integral, but instead integrate (what is now a vector valued integrand) over <math> \mathbb{R}^n </math>: if ''μ'' is a doubling measure on <math> \mathbb{R}^n </math> and
<math display="block"> \int_{|x|>1}\frac{1}{|x|}\,d\mu(x)<\infty</math>
then the map
<math display="block"> f(x) = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left(\frac{x-y}{|x-y|}+\frac{y}{|y|}\right)\,d\mu(y)</math>
is quasisymmetric (in fact, it is ''δ''-monotone for some ''δ'' depending on the measure ''μ'').<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = Kovalev | first1 = Leonid | last2 = Maldonado | first2 =  Diego | last3 = Wu | first3 = Jang-Mei | author3-link= Jang-Mei Wu | title = Doubling measures, monotonicity, and quasiconformality |journal= Math. Z. | volume = 257 | year = 2007 | number = 3 | pages = 525–545 | arxiv=math/0611110 | doi=10.1007/s00209-007-0132-5| s2cid = 119716883 }}</ref>

==Quasisymmetry and quasiconformality in Euclidean space==

Let <math>\Omega</math> and <math>\Omega'</math> be open subsets of <math> \mathbb{R}^n </math>. If <math> f\colon \Omega\to\Omega' </math> is ''η''-quasisymmetric, then it is also ''K''-[[quasiconformal]], where <math>K>0</math> is a constant depending on <math>\eta</math>.

Conversely, if <math> f\colon \Omega\to\Omega' </math> is ''K''-quasiconformal and <math>B(x,2r)</math> is contained in <math>\Omega</math>, then <math>f</math> is ''η''-quasisymmetric on <math>B(x,2r)</math>, where <math>\eta</math> depends only on <math>K</math>.

==Quasi-Möbius maps==
A related but weaker condition is the notion of quasi-Möbius maps where instead of the ratio only the cross-ratio is considered:<ref>{{cite book| last1 = Buyalo| first1 = Sergei | last2 = Schroeder | first2 = Viktor| title = Elements of Asymptotic Geometry | series = EMS Monographs in Mathematics | publisher = American Mathematical Society |  year = 2007 | pages = 209 | isbn = 978-3-03719-036-4}}</ref>

===Definition===

Let <math>(X,d_X)</math> and <math> (Y,d_Y) </math> be two [[metric space]]s and let <math> \eta:[0,+\infty) \to [0,+\infty) </math> be an increasing function. An '''''η''-quasi-Möbius''' [[homeomorphism]] <math> f\colon X\to Y </math>  is a homeomorphism such that for every quadruple <math> x,y,z,t </math>  of distinct points in <math> X </math>, we have

<math display="block"> \frac{d_Y(f(x),f(z))d_Y(f(y),f(t))}{d_Y(f(x),f(y))d_Y(f(z),f(t))} \leq \eta\left(\frac{d_X(x,z)d_X(y,t)}{d_X(x,y)d_X(z,t)}\right). </math>
